In this chapter we'll develop our understanding of hypothesis testing by exploring some related concepts: effect size, inferential errors, and statistical power. These are nuanced ideas, and statistical power in particular can be difficult to get your head around both conceptual and computationally. But they are key to fully understanding the strengths and limitations of hypothesis testing, so we'll take our time with them here before moving on to other ideas and tests.

## NHST logic recap

First, let's recap the ideas we covered in the previous chapter as a way of refining our thinking and preparing for the new aspects we'll examine. We'll do so in a different way than before, not by looking at a single dataset or one boring old curve. Instead we'll use something more dynamic, more charming, more fuzzy and yellow.

::::: {.callout-tip .interactive}
## Watch chance at work: the bee swarm

{{< interactive-figure beeSwarmAlpha makeBeeSwarm options='{"seed":"bee-swarm-alpha-v24","variability":"medium","n":50,"hiveOffset":0,"playing":false}' fallback="Animated bee swarm illustrating sampling variability and the five percent Type I error rate: bees flock around a fixed hive, each instant's mean position forms one sample mean, and over time about five percent of those means land in the critical regions even though the hive never moves." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-major="swarm" data-major-title="Swarm" data-title="The swarm" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":false,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":false}'}
It's a swarm of bees! Well, a simulated swarm: little yellow circles following a flocking algorithm. But aren't they charming? Watch them buzz this way and that for a moment. They try not to bump into each other. And they always know where their hive is. They venture away, but always return.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="swarm" data-major-title="Swarm" data-title="The swarm" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":false,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":false}'}
What does this have to do with null hypothesis significance testing, you may ask. Well, the hive at the center is the population mean, $\mu$. It is the real and unchanging center. The bees buzzing around it are a sample. The sample gives us a clue about the population---where is the hive? But the sample is constantly changing, as if we're drawing repeated samples. 
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="sampling" data-major-title="Sampling" data-title="One sample" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":false,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
We can freeze time. At this instant, the dashed line marks the average horizontal position of all the bees together: their sample mean, $M$. (We'll only care about horizontal position; the up-and-down motion is just for show.) It's close to the hive, but not exactly on it. That's sampling error.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="sampling" data-major-title="Sampling" data-title="One sample" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":false,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
Now, what if we didn't know for sure where the hive was? I've hidden it, but it still exists and hasn't changed. We can only see the sample mean, $M$. If we were to use that as our estimate of the population mean, we would be wrong.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="sampling" data-major-title="Sampling" data-title="One sample" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":false,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
When we're really testing hypotheses, we don't know the true population mean. We create our null hypothesis as a guess, a model of the world in which the population mean is whatever the null says it is. I've replaced the hive with a dashed outline representing our null hypothesis about the hive's position. It so happens that we're exactly right; the null predicts that the hive is where it really is.
:::

New step, showing the null curve and critical regions: So now we can describe the sampling distribution of the mean derived from that null hypothesis (its guess about the population center, as well as knowledge of the population variability, sample size, and normality). We set alpha (here .05) and define the critical regions. When a sample mean is in those regions, we would reject the null---wrongly!

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="sampling" data-major-title="Sampling" data-title="Every instant" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":false,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
Let's let the swarm get back to work, giving us sixty samples per second. The mean jitters around the hive, occasionally straying quite far away but generally staying close to the hidden hive. Occasionally it is far enough away that we would reject the null. Remember, we know that the null here is true, so those rejections are false alarms. 
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="sampling" data-major-title="Sampling" data-title="Collect" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":3600,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":false,"show-critical-regions":false,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":false,"animate":true}'}
Let's keep track of the sample means, building a histogram of their positions over time. The false alarms happen about five percent of the time, which is exactly what we expect with an $\alpha$ of .05.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="alpha" data-major-title="Alpha" data-title="Type I errors" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":false,"advance":3600,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Every one of those rejections was a false alarm — a type one error. That is what $\alpha = .05$ really means: when nothing is going on, chance alone will still cry wolf about five percent of the time.
:::

New step: Now, what if the null is wrong. I'm going to show the hive again, and also move it over a bit. So now the null---the dashed outline---is wrong about where the true population center is. This changes our logic a bit. Rather than risking falsely reject a correct null, we need to think about how likely it is we will *correctly* reject this wrong null. And on the other hand, what are the chances we will faile to reject the null, another kind of mistake.

New step: This will depend on a few things. First, how far away is the true population mean from the null? Second, how variable is the population? Third, how many bees are in our sample? And fourth, what alpha level have we set for our test? All of these factors will affect the probability that we will correctly reject the null hypothesis when it is false. This probability is called the statistical power of the test.
::::

:::::

The last step gives us a few things we need to nail down to flesh out our understanding of hypothesis testing, and an outline for the rest of this chapter. The distance between the null and the actual hive---more generically, the difference between the null and alternative population means---is called the *effect size*. The kinds of correct decisions and mistakes we can make are also important to consider. We can precisely quantify the long-run probability of making each type of decision, given our test assumptions and parameters. This will lead us to the concept of *statistical power*.

## Effect Size

Suppose you run a hypothesis test on some data and find a significant result, like we in [Chapter @sec-spider-test]. That means that the sample mean we found was sufficiently unlikely to have come from the null hypothesis distribution that we rejected the null hypothesis. In other words, the significance of the test tells us how (im)probable the result was. But it does not tell us how *big* of a difference it was, at least not directly.

First we need to talk about effect size. The procedure we worked through for the $z$ test at the end of the previous lecture led us to declare a "statistically significant" result. That means that the sample mean we found was sufficiently unlikely to have come from the null hypothesis distribution, according to our arbitrary criterion of $\alpha = .05$ or whatever it was, and so we rejected that null hypothesis. In other words, the significance of the test told us how (im)probable the result was. But it did not tell us how *big* of a difference it was, at least not directly.

That difference is part of the $z$ equation, of course. It's right there in the numerator, $X - \mu$. But we divide that numerator by the standard error of the mean, which is a function of the sample size: $\sigma_M = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. So as sample size increases, the standard error decreases, and even a small difference can become statistically significant, in the sense of being highly unlikely under the null hypothesis. On the other hand, a very large absolute difference in the numerator might turn out to be nonsignificant if we have a very small sample size, because the small $n$ will result in a relatively large denominator for the test statistic.

This can be a little confusing because in everyday language, calling something "significant" usually means it is big or important. But that's not what *statistical* significance means. Small, even trivial differences can be statistically significant. In particular, with a large enough sample size, even a tiny difference can be statistically significant. And that's because increasing sample size decreases the standard error of the mean, because sample size is in the denominator of the standard error equation, and a small standard error makes even very small differences quite improbable.

In sum, the significance of the test is only part of the story. Knowing how (im)probable the result was is important, but we also need to know the size of the difference we found. For that, we need a measure of *effect size*: a way of quantifying the absolute magnitude of a treatment effect, independent of sample size and statistical significance.

The trouble is, very small differences might be real, but not very important to us. So we need to consider effect size as well. Effect size tells us how big the treatment effect is in absolute terms, independent of sample size or statistical significance. In simple terms, you can think of effect size as the distance between the population means.

### Cohen's $d$

A common measure of effect size is Cohen's $d$ or difference score. Again, its purpose is to quantify the absolute magnitude of a treatment effect independent of sample size. And it does this by dividing the difference between means by the population standard deviation. 

$$ \begin{aligned} d &= \frac{\text{mean difference}}{\text{standard deviation}} \\[6pt] &= \frac{M - \mu}{\sigma} \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-cohens-d}

So essentially, it's a ratio. The numerator is the difference between means. The denominator is the population variability. The equation comes in slightly different forms for different tests, but for the $z$ test, it is the mean difference over the standard deviation, or our treated sample mean minus the original population mean divided by the population standard deviation $\sigma$. Notice that while the standard error, $\sigma_M$, varies with sample size, the population standard deviation, $\sigma$, does not. It is what it is. So Cohen's $d$ is independent of sample size.

So effect size is fairly easy to calculate. As for how to interpret it, Cohen outlined some rough rules of thumb, whereby a Cohen's $d$ of .2 would generally be considered a small effect, .5 would be considered medium, and .8 large. However, Cohen himself and many others have noted that these rules of thumb may not apply in all situations.

For a beautiful interactive visualization of what different values of Cohen's $d$ actually look like, spend some time with [Kristoffer Magnusson's effect-size visualization](https://rpsychologist.com/cohend/).


### Effect size and significance

Let's demonstrate the difference between significance and effect size. Suppose we're educational psychologists trying to develop an intervention to boost children's SAT scores. And suppose we think we've hit upon an effective treatment: giving the test taker a banana just before taking the test. Maybe the potassium helps with cognitive function or something like that. SAT scores have a population mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 100. And since we know that standard deviation, we know a $z$ test would be an appropriate hypothesis test.

So we administer the banana treatment to a sample of test takers and we find the sample mean to be 501. We want to know if this is statistically significant with an $\alpha$ of .05 two-tailed, giving us critical values of $\pm 1.96$.

$$ z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma_M} = \frac{501 - 500}{100 / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{1}{100 / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{\sqrt{n}}{100} $$

But we also want to know if it is a meaningful effect, if it's big enough for us to care about. So we need to calculate the effect size as well.

$$ d = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{501 - 500}{100} = \frac{1}{100} = 0.01 $$


First, let's suppose the results came from a sample of 50 students.

{{< include quizzes/09-power-significance-effect-size.qmd >}}

See if you can calculate the $z$ score to determine significance and Cohen's $d$ to quantify the effect size. 


Now let's suppose that it came from a sample of fifty thousand students, and calculate the $z$ score and Cohen's $d$ again.

In the first case, with just 50 participants, we were not able to reject the null hypothesis of no difference. Our hypothesis test was non-significant and Cohen's $d$ came out at .01, an absolutely trivial difference. With 50,000 participants, however, the hypothesis test did lead us to reject the null hypothesis. The sample mean of 501 now seemed sufficiently unlikely that we could reject the null hypothesis. Again, this is because sample size determines the standard error, the denominator of the test statistic. So as sample size increases, we become more likely to find a significant difference, all else being equal. But you should have gotten exactly the same answer for Cohen's $d$. It is still a trivial effect, even if it's real. The measure of effect size tells us that because it is independent of sample size.

So based on the results of the significance test, we might be tempted to invest in supplying every schoolchild with a banana before every test they take. But the measure of effect size tells us that probably would not be a sensible use of resources. The tiny effect just wouldn't justify the effort of the treatment.


### Interpreting Effect Size

What does a difference of half a standard deviation actually look like? Here, we'll picture two populations of individual scores. For simplicity, both distributions are normal and have the same standard deviation. Moving one mean changes the effect size while leaving the variability within each population alone.

::::: {#act-cohens-d .callout-tip .interactive .with-controls}
## Explore Cohen's d

{{< interactive-figure effectSizeTutorial makeEffectSizeTutorial fallback="Explore Cohen's d. Use the accompanying steps for an explanation." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A small difference" data-action='{"d":0.2,"overlap":false}'}
The dashed population has a mean just $0.2$ standard deviations above the solid one. That's the distance Cohen called a small effect. We're picturing a population difference here; the $d$ we calculate from sample data is an estimate of that difference. These curves show individual scores, not the sampling distributions of sample means.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A larger difference" data-action='{"d":0.5,"overlap":false}'}
At $d = 0.5$, the means are half a standard deviation apart. The dashed curve has moved, but neither curve has narrowed. That's the idea behind standardizing the difference: we're asking how far apart the means are relative to the variability among individual scores. We haven't changed the sample size or calculated a significance test.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Large still overlaps" data-action='{"d":0.8,"overlap":true}'}
Now set $d = 0.8$, Cohen's rough benchmark for a large effect, and shade the area shared by the two curves. They still overlap by about 69 percent! A substantial difference between means can coexist with a lot of individual variation. Knowing which population a person belongs to wouldn't tell us exactly what their score is.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Explore the overlap" data-action='{"controls-open":true,"d":0.8,"overlap":true}'}
Move the slider toward zero, then toward larger differences. The shared area shrinks as the means move apart. This percentage describes the area under both curves, relative to the area under either one; it isn't the percentage of people unaffected by a treatment. And it depends on the normal, equal-SD shapes we're using here. An effect size alone doesn't determine the overlap for every possible pair of distributions.
:::

::::
:::::

So the labels *small*, *medium*, and *large* need some care. Whether a difference matters depends on what we're measuring, what it costs to produce the change, and what its consequences are. A small difference can matter a great deal when it affects many people or accumulates over time. We'll return to some concrete examples later in this chapter.

## Errors in Hypothesis Testing

Null hypothesis significance testing is an inferential process, by which I mean we're using limited information from a sample to make a general conclusion about a population. Hopefully we make the correct decision. But because we don't have direct insight into what's really true in the world, we only have our limited and imperfect inferences to work with, it's possible to make the wrong decision.

There are two decisions we can make: either we accept or reject the null hypothesis. And there are two actual states of affairs in reality, though, again, we can never have perfect direct knowledge of which one is true. Either the null hypothesis really is true or it really is false.

So there are four possible outcomes in total. Hopefully, we accept the null hypothesis when it really is true — concluding that there is no effect, when really there isn't. And hopefully we reject the null hypothesis when it really is false, concluding that there is an effect when there really is.

### Type I Error (False Positive)

But there is a chance that we will reject the null hypothesis when we shouldn't have, when it actually is true. In other words, we might think that there is an effect when there actually isn't. This is called, entirely unhelpfully, a type one error. A more useful description would be a false positive: thinking that there is an effect when actually there isn't.

### Type II Error (False Negative)

And there's a chance that we will fail to reject the null hypothesis when we should have rejected it, when it is actually false, and there really is an effect. We just failed to find convincing evidence of it. This is called a type two error or a false negative: thinking that there is no effect when really there is.

### $\alpha$ and the Type I Error Rate

The type one error, the false positive, is actually just another name for $\alpha$, the probability that we set as our cutoff criterion for unlikely results. If you think about it, an $\alpha$ of .05, say, is an admission that if the null hypothesis is correct, we would see sample means like this five percent of the time. If we ran our experiment 100 times, even if there is no treatment effect, we would mistakenly reject our null hypothesis five out of those 100 times. So this is basically saying that five percent of samples that come from the null hypothesis sampling distribution will cause us to mistakenly reject the null hypothesis. We're going to be wrong five percent of the time.

The argument in favor of this is that five percent is sufficiently low that we can live with that risk of a type one false positive error. But there are good arguments that five percent is too high and that we should more often use a lower $\alpha$ value of 1 percent or even .1 percent in order to reduce the chances of making a type one error. That's an ongoing debate and one you might hear more about in more advanced research methods or stats classes.

### $\beta$ and the Type II Error Rate

The type two error — the false negative, or failing to reject the null hypothesis that is false, or put another way, failing to detect a real effect — is referred to as $\beta$. And you might think that $\beta$ is just the flip side of $\alpha$, but it's a bit more complicated than that. $\beta$ is related to the statistical power of a hypothesis test. We'll cover that in more detail later in this lecture.

### Remembering the Difference

Now, it's too bad that "type one" and "type two" are such uninformative names because this is a very important concept. One way to try and remember them is to remember that the villagers in the story of the boy who cried wolf made a type one error and a type two error in that order. At first, there was no wolf, just a mischievous young shepherd who cried wolf. The villagers made a false positive mistake. They thought there was a wolf and there wasn't. And the next time there was a wolf, the boy cried wolf again. But this time, the villagers made a false negative, failing to detect the wolf that really was there.

## Statistical Power

Moving on to statistical power, the power of a test is defined as the probability that the test will reject the null hypothesis if the treatment really does have an effect. If a treatment really does have an effect, we're focusing on the right-hand column of the table here, under which $H_0$ is false. 

<div class="table-responsive">
<table id="inf-tab">
  <thead>
     <tr><th colspan=2 style="border-bottom: none;"></th><th colspan=2 style="text-align: center;">Actual situation</th></tr>
     <tr><th colspan=2></th><th style="text-align: center;">$H_0$ true</th><th style="text-align: center; background-color: #B3D1E3;">$H_0$ false</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td rowspan=2 style="writing-mode: vertical-rl; transform: rotate(180deg); text-align: center; font-weight: bold;">Researcher's<br>Decision</td>
      <td style="text-align: right; font-weight: bold;" >Reject $H_0$</td>
      <td style="text-align: center; color: red; border-color: var(--text-color);">Type 1 error<br>$\alpha$</td>
      <td style="text-align: center; color: #50C878; border-color: var(--text-color); background-color: #B3D1E3;">Correct<br>$1-\beta$</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td style="text-align: right; font-weight: bold;" >Fail to reject $H_0$</td>
      <td style="text-align: center; color: #50C878; border-color: var(--text-color);">Correct</td>
      <td style="text-align: center; color: red; border-color: var(--text-color); background-color: #B3D1E3; background-opacity: 0.5;">Type 2 error<br>$\beta$</td>  
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
</div>

There are two possible outcomes: either we fail to reject the null hypothesis, making a type two false negative error; or we correctly reject the null hypothesis. Because these two complementary outcomes cover the whole probability space, their probabilities must add up to 1. The probability of a type two error is referred to as $\beta$. Therefore, the other outcome, the correct rejection of the null, must have a probability of $1 - \beta$. This quantity, $1 - \beta$, is the statistical power of the test.



### Calculating Power

::::: {#act-calculating-power .callout-tip .interactive .with-controls}
## Explore statistical power

{{< interactive-figure statisticalPower makeStatisticalPowerDiagram options='{"mu":50,"sigma":10,"n":25,"d":0.5,"alpha":0.05,"showAlt":false,"axisZNull":true,"axisRaw":false}' fallback="Explore statistical power. Use the accompanying steps for an explanation." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-title="The null" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":10,"n":25,"effect-size":0.5,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"show-H1":false,"raw-scores":false,"h0-z":true,"h1-z":false}'}
Start with a null population mean of 50, a population SD of 10, and samples of 25. The standard error is $10 / \sqrt{25} = 2$. This curve shows sample means under the null, labeled in $z$ units. For a two-tailed test with $\alpha = .05$, the critical $z$ values are about $\pm 1.96$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Critical means" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":10,"n":25,"effect-size":0.5,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"show-H1":false,"raw-scores":true,"h0-z":true,"h1-z":false}'}
On the raw-score ruler, those same boundaries are $50 - 1.96(2) = 46.08$ and $50 + 1.96(2) = 53.92$. Sample means outside these boundaries lead us to reject the null. Keep those raw-score boundaries in mind: we will use the same decision rule when we consider a population where the null is false.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="A specified alternative" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":10,"n":25,"effect-size":0.5,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"show-H1":true,"raw-scores":true,"h0-z":false,"h1-z":false}'}
Suppose the true population mean is 55 instead. That's a difference of five points, or $d = 0.5$, because the population SD is 10. Samples of 25 from this alternative population have a sampling distribution centered on 55, still with a standard error of 2. The violet areas show the sample means that would cross the null's rejection boundaries.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="The alternative ruler" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":10,"n":25,"effect-size":0.5,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"show-H1":true,"raw-scores":true,"h0-z":false,"h1-z":true}'}
Now read the boundaries relative to the alternative mean. The lower one is $(46.08 - 55) / 2 = -4.46$ standard errors below it; the upper one is $(53.92 - 55) / 2 = -0.54$. The boundaries are still at the same raw scores. We've changed the ruler we use to describe them.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Misses and detections" data-action='{"mu":50,"sigma":10,"n":25,"effect-size":0.5,"alpha":0.05,"two-tailed":true,"show-H1":true,"raw-scores":true,"h0-z":false,"h1-z":true}'}
The gray area under the alternative curve lies between the critical boundaries. These samples fail to reject a false null: $\beta \approx .295$. The violet area outside the boundaries is power: $1 - \beta \approx .705$. So this design detects this particular effect about 71 percent of the time over repeated studies. Both rejection tails count, though the far-left contribution here is tiny.
:::

::::
:::::

We'll work through calculating power both visually and mathematically. Visually, here's our null hypothesis distribution with critical regions highlighted red. As you know by now, these critical regions are the regions of the sampling distribution that will cause us to reject the null hypothesis. So to think about statistical power, we need to imagine what the alternative hypothesis distribution with its different mean would look like, and how it overlaps with the null distribution. Specifically, what proportion of sample means for the alternative hypothesis distribution fall within the critical regions of the null distribution and will cause us to reject the null hypothesis? That is the power of the test, the region shaded violet here.

This is slightly complicated to think about. So we'll work through it step by step. First, we focus on the null distribution. We need to determine the critical $z$ scores that define those red critical regions. Since we're dealing with a normal distribution, we know that we can use the unit normal table to find those scores. So let's say our $\alpha$ is .05. We'd find critical $z$ scores of $\pm 1.96$.

{{< interactive-figure powerCriticalZTable makeCriticalValueTable options='{"distribution":"normal","layout":"areas","title":"Unit normal table (excerpt)","z":{"from":1.92,"to":2.0,"step":0.01},"zDigits":2,"areas":["left","right","mean-to-z"],"selected":{"z":1.96,"area":"right"},"maxWidth":"32rem"}' fallback="Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 1.92 to 2.00, with the area to the right of z = 1.96, .0250, highlighted." >}}

The next step is to determine what original sample means those critical $z$ scores correspond to. That requires knowing the null distribution's mean and variability. So let's say the population mean is 50 with a standard deviation of 10. We know from the central limit theorem that this sampling distribution will also have a mean of 50, and its variability, the standard error of the mean, is found by dividing the standard deviation by the square root of the sample size. So let's say our sample size is 25.

<!-- [Note: Original lecture included an interactive element here.] -->

See if you can calculate the critical means.

{{< include quizzes/09-power-critical-means.qmd >}}

Next, we turn our attention to the alternative hypothesis distribution. We need to know what effect size to expect. So in other words, how much higher or lower is the mean of the alternative distribution than the original distribution? Let's say we expect a difference of five points.

<!-- [Note: Original lecture included an interactive element here.] -->

Now we need to work out what $z$ scores correspond to the sample means we just worked out, but for this distribution.

{{< include quizzes/09-power-alternative-means.qmd >}}

So we plug the relevant values into the $z$ equation to work out each value. See if you can get them. Now we can find the proportion of the alternative distribution that falls between those $z$ scores. Using the unit normal table, we subtract the area to the left of the lower boundary from the area to the left of the upper boundary. The area to the left of $z = -0.54$ is the same as the area to the right of $z = 0.54$, which the table gives as .2946, and the area to the left of $z = -4.46$ is so far out in the tail that it rounds to .0000: $.2946 - .0000 = .2946$. This gives us the area of the region shaded gray here. This is the proportion of the alternative distribution that will cause us to fail to reject the null hypothesis, making a type two, false negative error. Remember, we refer to this quantity as $\beta$.

{{< interactive-figure powerBetaZTable makeCriticalValueTable options='{"distribution":"normal","layout":"areas","title":"Unit normal table (excerpt)","z":{"from":0.5,"to":0.58,"step":0.01},"zDigits":2,"areas":["left","right","mean-to-z"],"selected":{"z":0.54,"area":"right"},"maxWidth":"32rem"}' fallback="Excerpt of the unit normal table for z from 0.50 to 0.58, with the area to the right of z = 0.54, .2946, highlighted." >}}

And so finally we can work out the statistical power of the test — the chances of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis — by working out the area of the rest of the distribution. This is just $1 - \beta$, because it has to add up to 1. So for this example, we had a 29.5% chance of making a type two error, leaving us with a 70.5% chance of making the correct decision to reject the null hypothesis. So the power of the test is .705.

Given our stated sample size here, and population standard deviations and means, if we could run this experiment 100 times, we would successfully reject our null hypothesis 70.5% of the time.

### Factors Affecting Power

It's worth spending some time thinking this through, particularly thinking about how changing different quantities will affect statistical power. Increasing effect size, the distance between the means, increases power because the distributions will be farther apart and overlap less. Increasing sample size also increases power because it reduces the standard error, again meaning that the distributions will overlap less. Reducing our $\alpha$ value lowers power because it makes for a more stringent test. The critical regions of the null distribution will be smaller and so less of the alternative distribution will cause us to reject the null. And the directionality of our hypothesis affects power as well. Using a one-tailed test increases power since it gives a larger critical region in one tail that we're interested in.

If you really understand how and why each of these factors affects power, you'll have a good grasp of the concept.

::::: {.callout-tip .interactive}
## Watch power in action: the swarm returns

{{< interactive-figure beeSwarmPower makeBeeSwarm options='{"seed":"bee-swarm-power-v3","variability":"medium","n":50,"hiveOffset":0,"playing":false}' fallback="Animated bee swarm illustrating statistical power: when the hive moves away from the null position, the proportion of sample means that land in the critical regions is the power of the test, and it rises with sample size and effect size and falls with variability." >}}

:::: {.callout-footer}
::: {.tutorial-step data-major="null" data-major-title="Null true" data-title="Null true" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":0,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":3600,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":false,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":false}'}
The swarm again, with everything in view. The hive sits exactly where the null hypothesis says it should, so the sample means pile onto the null distribution — and the roughly 5% that land in the critical regions are all false alarms.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="effect" data-major-title="Effect" data-title="Move the hive" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":10,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":0,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Now the hive has moved; the dashed marker shows where the null hypothesis still thinks it is. The null is false — there is a real effect of $d =$ {{< interactive-value beeSwarmPower.d format=".2f" >}} — but our critical regions stay right where they were.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="effect" data-major-title="Effect" data-title="Power" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":10,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":3600,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Rebuild the pile of sample means. It centers on the true hive, not on the null — and now a sample mean in the critical region is a good thing: a correct detection of the real effect. The proportion of the time that happens is the power of the test: {{< interactive-value beeSwarmPower.proportionSignificant format=".3f" >}}.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="factors" data-major-title="Factors" data-title="More bees" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":100,"hive-offset":10,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":3600,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Give the swarm 100 bees instead of 50. More bees per sample means a smaller standard error, a tighter pile of means, less overlap with the null — and more power: {{< interactive-value beeSwarmPower.proportionSignificant format=".3f" >}}.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="factors" data-major-title="Factors" data-title="More noise" data-action='{"variability":"high","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":10,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":3600,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Crank the variability instead. A noisier swarm inflates the standard error, so the same 10-pixel effect is now small relative to the noise, and sample means rarely clear the critical bounds. Power sinks back toward $\alpha$: {{< interactive-value beeSwarmPower.proportionSignificant format=".3f" >}}.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="factors" data-major-title="Factors" data-title="Bigger effect" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":20,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":3600,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"animate":true}'}
Finally, move the hive farther out. A bigger effect is simply easier to see — hardly any sample means stay inside the null's bounds now: {{< interactive-value beeSwarmPower.proportionSignificant format=".3f" >}}.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="factors" data-major-title="Factors" data-title="Explore" data-action='{"variability":"medium","sample-size":50,"hive-offset":20,"alpha":0.05,"playing":true,"advance":3600,"show-swarm":true,"show-hive":true,"show-null-hive":true,"show-mean-line":true,"show-null-curve":true,"show-critical-regions":true,"show-histogram":true,"show-significance-tracker":true,"controls-open":true,"animate":true}'}
Now it's yours. Mix the three ingredients — sample size, variability, and effect size (the hive offset) — and watch what each one does to the power tracker. (The fourth factor, $\alpha$, stays fixed at .05 here.)
:::

For another way to build intuition about how these factors interact, explore [Kristoffer Magnusson's interactive NHST/power visualization](https://rpsychologist.com/d3/NHST/).

### Practical Applications of Power

Since this is all quite abstract, you may be wondering the usefulness of knowing about statistical power. And honestly, it has long been overlooked within psychology. Until recently, it was quite rare for a published research paper to even mention statistical power. But it's now generally accepted that power should be a central feature of research design.

Researchers could calculate the power of a study before beginning their research or after a study has been conducted, using their knowledge or their assumptions about effect size, sample size, and $\alpha$. But a more practically useful use of power is to specify the power you want in advance and adjust your required sample size in order to achieve that level of power. This requires knowing or estimating your expected effect size. And then you can say, for example, that you want a power of .8 or an 80 percent chance of detecting a real effect of that size. And then you can calculate how many participants you need in order to achieve that level of power.

### Power in Context: Real-World Examples

To put these ideas in context, @simmons2013life compared some familiar differences and the sample sizes needed to detect them with 80 percent power.

These examples compare two groups. We haven't introduced the test for that design yet, but we can still picture the standardized distance between their means. Select a row to see its effect size. The curves are illustrations using normal distributions with equal SDs, not reconstructions of the original data. The comparison mean is placed to the right to show the size of the difference; this doesn't identify which named group scored higher.

{{< interactive-figure effectSizeExamples makeEffectSizeTutorial options='{"d":1.85,"overlap":true,"examples":[{"group":"Gender","label":"Height","d":1.85,"n":"6"},{"group":"Liberal / Conservative","label":"Importance of social equality","d":0.69,"n":"34"},{"group":"Like eggs / dislike eggs","label":"Frequency of eating egg salad","d":0.58,"n":"48"},{"group":"Smoker / nonsmoker","label":"Estimated risk of smoking-related death","d":0.33,"n":"144"},{"group":"Prefer science / prefer art","label":"Number of planets named correctly","d":0.07,"n":"3,669"}]}' fallback="Selectable effect-size examples, from d = 1.85 for height to d = 0.07 for naming planets." >}}

The effect sizes and sample sizes shown are the examples reported by @simmons2013life for 80 percent power; $n$ is **per group**. The figure displays the effect sizes, not a new power calculation. In particular, these sample sizes don't belong to the one-sample $z$ test we used above.

So, for example, given the real average difference between men and women's heights, you'd need around twelve people, six men and six women, to have sufficient statistical power to detect it. The difference between men and women's heights is very large, with a Cohen's $d$ of around 1.85. So you don't need many participants to reliably detect it.

Usually, though, psychologists are interested in more subtle differences. You might think the difference between liberals and conservatives in terms of how important they say social equality is would be pretty robust. But given its effect size of around .7, you already need many more participants, around 34 each of liberals and conservatives, or almost 70 participants total, in order to have a power of .8 to detect the difference.

This paper also included some questions that sound kind of funny, like comparing people who say they do or do not like eggs in terms of how often they eat egg salad. You'd think this would be a pretty easy effect to detect, but you'd need close to 100 participants to reliably detect it.

A lot of psychology has to do with attitudes and behaviors that we aren't entirely aware of, like motivated cognition. It seems pretty plausible that smokers would underestimate the likelihood of a smoker dying from a smoking-related illness as compared to nonsmokers. And they do. But it's a small enough effect that you'd need almost 300 people in your study to detect it with 80 percent power.

And lastly, people who say they prefer science over art can name more of the planets than people who say they prefer art. Again, it's plausible that this would be the case, but it's a very small difference. If you didn't know the size of the difference in advance, you'd need a study with more than 7,000 people to have 80 percent power to detect the difference.

So this is all worth bearing in mind when you read papers for other classes. Think about the sample sizes they had, the subtlety of the effects that they're looking for, and whether they really had sufficient power to detect those effects.

I'll end with a quote here by <!-- [Possible typo: "by its statistical power" in original; likely meant "about statistical power"] --> Stuart Ritchie from *Science Fictions*, which is a great recent book about the scientific method and the uses and misuses of statistics. The author noted that running a study with low statistical power is like setting out to look for distant galaxies with a pair of binoculars. Even if what you're looking for is definitely out there, you have essentially no chance of seeing it. And I would add, anything you do see may not be quite what you think it is.
